'''Michael J. Ware''' (born 1939, [[Bromley]]) {{postnominals|country=GBR|FRSC|FRSC}} is a chemist and photographer, known for his work in [[Alternative process|alternative photographic process]]es, earlier methods of printing photographic images that were succeeded by the more common silver-gelatin used today. In the Present, Ware acts as a consultant, most recently on the history and development of the platinotype and palladium processes. His has also written about chemistry's influence on the history of photography.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ware|first=Mike|date=2007-07-26|title=The enduring image|url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/the-enduring-image/3004827.article|access-date=2021-02-20|website=Chemistry World|language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Ware was born in 1939 in Bromley. He earned his Ph.D. at the [[University of Oxford]] in 1965. His thesis was ''The vibrational spectra of some inorganic complexes.''<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=The vibrational spectra of some inorganic complexes|url=https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.710758|publisher=University of Oxford|date=1965|degree=Ph.D.|first=M. J.|last=Ware}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
* 1982 Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry<ref>{{Cite web|title=MikeWare - Biographical Sketch|url=https://www.mikeware.co.uk/mikeware/Biographical.html|access-date=2021-02-20|website=www.mikeware.co.uk}}</ref>
* 1990 [[Hood Medal]], awarded by the Royal Photographic Society<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hood Medal|url=https://rps.org/about/awards/history-and-recipients/hood-medal/|access-date=2021-02-20|website=rps.org|language=en-GB}}</ref>
